o: Todo aquel día, esperando la noche, estuvieron en aquel lugar y mesón don Quijote y Sancho: el uno, para acabar en la campaña rasa la tanda de su diciplina, y el otro, para ver el fin della, en el cual consistía el de su deseo.
t: All that day, waiting for nightfall, Don Quixote and Sancho stayed at that inn and inn-yard: the one to finish in the open field the task of his discipline, and the other to see the end of it, which was the object of his desire.

o: Llegó en esto al mesón un caminante a caballo, con tres o cuatro criados, uno de los cuales dijo al que el señor dellos parecía.
t: Just then a traveler on horseback arrived at the inn, with three or four servants, one of whom spoke to the one who seemed to be their master.

o: — Aquí puede vuestra merced, señor don Álvaro Tarfe, pasar hoy la siesta: la posada parece limpia y fresca.
t: "Your worship, sir Don Álvaro Tarfe, may spend the siesta here today: the inn looks clean and cool."

o: Oyendo esto don Quijote, le dijo a Sancho.
t: Hearing this, Don Quixote said to Sancho.

o: — Mira, Sancho: cuando yo hojeé aquel libro de la segunda parte de mi historia, me parece que de pasada topé allí este nombre de don Álvaro Tarfe.
t: "Look, Sancho: when I leafed through that book of the second part of my history, it seems to me that I came across this name of Don Álvaro Tarfe in passing."

o: — Bien podrá ser —respondió Sancho—.
t: "It could well be," replied Sancho.

o: Dejémosle apear, que después se lo preguntaremos.
t: Let us have him dismount, and we will ask him about it afterward.

o: El caballero se apeó, y, frontero del aposento de don Quijote, la huéspeda le dio una sala baja, enjaezada con otras pintadas sargas, como las que tenía la estancia de don Quijote.
t: The gentleman dismounted, and opposite Don Quixote's room the innkeeper gave him a low chamber hung with other painted hangings, like those in Don Quixote's quarters.

o: Púsose el recién venido caballero a lo de verano, y, saliéndose al portal del mesón, que era espacioso y fresco, por el cual se paseaba don Quijote, le preguntó.
t: The newly arrived gentleman put himself in summer dress, and, coming out into the porch of the inn, which was spacious and cool, where Don Quixote was strolling, he asked him.

o: — ¿Adónde bueno camina vuestra merced, señor gentilhombre?
t: "Where is your worship headed, sir gentleman?"

o: Y don Quijote le respondió.
t: And Don Quixote replied to him.

o: — A una aldea que está aquí cerca, de donde soy natural.
t: "To a village near here, where I was born."

o: Y vuestra merced, ¿dónde camina?
t: And your worship, where are you bound?

o: — Yo, señor —respondió el caballero—, voy a Granada, que es mi patria.
t: "I, sir," replied the gentleman, "am going to Granada, which is my homeland."

o: — ¡Y buena patria!
t: "And a good homeland!"

o: —replicó don Quijote—.
t: "replied Don Quixote."

o: Pero, dígame vuestra merced, por cortesía, su nombre, porque me parece que me ha de importar saberlo más de lo que buenamente podré decir.
t: But, tell me your grace, if you please, your name, for it seems to me that it must matter more to me than I could ever properly say.

o: — Mi nombre es don Álvaro Tarfe —respondió el huésped.
t: "My name is Don Álvaro Tarfe," the guest replied.

o: A lo que replicó don Quijote.
t: To which Don Quixote responded.

o: — Sin duda alguna pienso que vuestra merced debe de ser aquel don Álvaro Tarfe que anda impreso en la Segunda parte de la historia de don Quijote de la Mancha, recién impresa y dada a la luz del mundo por un autor moderno.
t: "Without a doubt, I think your grace must be that Don Álvaro Tarfe who goes about in print in the Second Part of the story of Don Quixote of La Mancha, just published and brought to light by a modern author."

o: — Y, dígame vuestra merced, señor don Álvaro, ¿parezco yo en algo a ese tal don Quijote que vuestra merced dice?
t: "And tell me, your grace, sir Don Álvaro, do I resemble in any way that Don Quixote your grace speaks of?"

o: — No, por cierto —respondió el huésped—: en ninguna manera.
t: "No, certainly not," the guest replied; "in no way at all."

o: — Y ese don Quijote —dijo el nuestro—, ¿traía consigo a un escudero llamado Sancho Panza?
t: "And that Don Quixote," said ours, "did he have with him a squire named Sancho Panza?"

o: — Sí traía —respondió don Álvaro—; y, aunque tenía fama de muy gracioso, nunca le oí decir gracia que la tuviese.
t: "He did," Don Álvaro replied; "and though he had a great reputation for wit, I never once heard him say anything that was actually funny."

o: — ¡Por Dios que lo creo!
t: "By God, I believe it!"

o: —respondió don Álvaro—, porque más gracias habéis dicho vos, amigo, en cuatro razones que habéis hablado, que el otro Sancho Panza en cuantas yo le oí hablar, que fueron muchas.
t: Don Álvaro replied, "for you, friend, have said more graceful things in the four sentences you have spoken than the other Sancho Panza did in all the times I ever heard him talk, which were many."

o: Más tenía de comilón que de bien hablado, y más de tonto que de gracioso, y tengo por sin duda que los encantadores que persiguen a don Quijote el bueno han querido perseguirme a mí con don Quijote el malo.
t: He was more of a glutton than a good talker, and more of a fool than a wit, and I hold it beyond doubt that the enchanters who persecute the good Don Quixote have wanted to persecute me as well, along with the bad Don Quixote.

o: Pero no sé qué me diga; que osaré yo jurar que le dejo metido en la casa del Nuncio, en Toledo, para que le curen, y agora remanece aquí otro don Quijote, aunque bien diferente del mío.
t: But I don't know what to say; I would even swear that I have left him shut up in the Nuncio's house in Toledo, so that they can cure him, and now another Don Quixote turns up here, though quite different from mine.

o: Y, aunque los sucesos que en ella me han sucedido no son de mucho gusto, sino de mucha pesadumbre, los llevo sin ella, sólo por haberla visto.
t: And though the events that have befallen me in it are not very pleasant, but rather very burdensome, I bear them without it, solely for having seen her.

o: Finalmente, señor don Álvaro Tarfe, yo soy don Quijote de la Mancha, el mismo que dice la fama, y no ese desventurado que ha querido usurpar mi nombre y honrarse con mis pensamientos.
t: In short, sir Don Álvaro Tarfe, I am Don Quixote of La Mancha, the very one the fame speaks of, and not that unfortunate impostor who has wished to usurp my name and honor himself with my deeds.

o: A vuestra merced suplico, por lo que debe a ser caballero, sea servido de hacer una declaración ante el alcalde deste lugar, de que vuestra merced no me ha visto en todos los días de su vida hasta agora, y de que yo no soy el don Quijote impreso en la segunda parte, ni este Sancho Panza mi escudero es aquél que vuestra merced conoció.
t: I beseech your grace, by whatever you owe to being a gentleman, to be pleased to make a declaration before the magistrate of this place, that your grace has not seen me in all the days of your life until now, and that I am not the Don Quixote printed in the second part, nor is this Sancho Panza, my squire, the one your grace knew.

o: — Eso haré yo de muy buena gana —respondió don Álvaro—, puesto que cause admiración ver dos don Quijotes y dos Sanchos a un mismo tiempo, tan conformes en los nombres como diferentes en las acciones; y vuelvo a decir y me afirmo que no he visto lo que he visto, ni ha pasado por mí lo que ha pasado.
t: "I will do so very willingly," Don Álvaro replied, "since it causes wonder to see two Don Quixotes and two Sanchos at one and the same time, so alike in their names and so different in their deeds; and I say again and affirm that I have not seen what I have seen, nor has what has happened happened to me."

o: — Sin duda —dijo Sancho— que vuestra merced debe de estar encantado, como mi señora Dulcinea del Toboso, y pluguiera al cielo que estuviera su desencanto de vuestra merced en darme otros tres mil y tantos azotes como me doy por ella, que yo me los diera sin interés alguno.
t: "No doubt," said Sancho, "that your grace must be enchanted, like my lady Dulcinea of Toboso, and Heaven grant that your grace's disenchantment were worth as much to me as three thousand odd lashes more, which I would give on her behalf, and I would give them without any interest at all."

o: — No entiendo eso de azotes —dijo don Álvaro.
t: "I don't understand that business about lashes," said Don Álvaro.

o: Y Sancho le respondió que era largo de contar, pero que él se lo contaría si acaso iban un mesmo camino.
t: And Sancho replied that it was a long story, but that he would tell it to him in case they were traveling the same road.

o: Llegóse en esto la hora de comer; comieron juntos don Quijote y don Álvaro.
t: At this moment the hour of eating arrived; Don Quixote and Don Álvaro ate together.

o: Finalmente, el alcalde proveyó jurídicamente; la declaración se hizo con todas las fuerzas que en tales casos debían hacerse, con lo que quedaron don Quijote y Sancho muy alegres, como si les importara mucho semejante declaración y no mostrara claro la diferencia de los dos don Quijotes y la de los dos Sanchos sus obras y sus palabras.
t: In the end, the mayor provided legal proof; the declaration was made with all the formality such cases required, which left Don Quixote and Sancho very happy, as though such a declaration mattered greatly to them and it were not clear from the difference between the two Don Quixotes and the two Sanchos, their deeds and their words.

o: Muchas de cortesías y ofrecimientos pasaron entre don Álvaro y don Quijote, en las cuales mostró el gran manchego su discreción, de modo que desengañó a don Álvaro Tarfe del error en que estaba; el cual se dio a entender que debía de estar encantado, pues tocaba con la mano dos tan contrarios don Quijotes.
t: Many courtesies and offers passed between Don Álvaro and Don Quixote, in which the great Manchegan showed his discretion, so that he disabused Don Álvaro Tarfe of the error he was in; who gave himself to understand that he must be enchanted, since he had with his own hand touched two such contrary Don Quixotes.

o: Llegó la tarde, partiéronse de aquel lugar, y a obra de media legua se apartaban dos caminos diferentes, el uno que guiaba a la aldea de don Quijote, y el otro el que había de llevar don Álvaro.
t: Afternoon arrived, they took leave of that place, and about half a league on two different roads branched off, one leading to Don Quixote's village, and the other the one that was to carry Don Álvaro.

o: No perdió el engañado don Quijote un solo golpe de la cuenta, y halló que con los de la noche pasada era tres mil y veinte y nueve.
t: The deceived Don Quixote did not miss a single blow of the reckoning, and found that together with those of the night before it came to three thousand and twenty-nine.

o: Parece que había madrugado el sol a ver el sacrificio, con cuya luz volvieron a proseguir su camino, tratando entre los dos del engaño de don Álvaro y de cuán bien acordado había sido tomar su declaración ante la justicia, y tan auténticamente.
t: It seems the sun had risen early to see the sacrifice, and by its light they went on their way, the two of them discussing the deception of Don Álvaro and how well it had been arranged to have their declaration taken before the justice, and so authentically.

o: Con estos pensamientos y deseos subieron una cuesta arriba, desde la cual descubrieron su aldea, la cual, vista de Sancho, se hincó de rodillas y dijo.
t: With these thoughts and wishes they climbed a slope, from which they discovered their village, which, seen by Sancho, brought him to his knees, and he said:

o: — Abre los ojos, deseada patria, y mira que vuelve a ti Sancho Panza, tu hijo, si no muy rico, muy bien azotado.
t: "Open your eyes, dearest homeland, and see that Sancho Panza, your son, returns to you, if not very rich, very well beaten."

o: Abre los brazos y recibe también tu hijo don Quijote, que si viene vencido de los brazos ajenos, viene vencedor de sí mismo; que, según él me ha dicho, es el mayor vencimiento que desearse puede.
t: Open your arms and receive also your son Don Quixote, who, if he comes vanquished by others' arms, comes victorious over himself; for, as he has told me, that is the greatest victory that can be desired.

o: Dineros llevo, porque si buenos azotes me daban, bien caballero me iba.
t: I bring money, because if they were giving me good blows, I was playing the gentleman very well.

o: — Déjate desas sandeces —dijo don Quijote—, y vamos con pie derecho a entrar en nuestro lugar, donde daremos vado a nuestras imaginaciones, y la traza que en la pastoral vida pensamos ejercitar.
t: "Leave your fooleries," said Don Quixote, "and let's set off straight to enter our village, where we will give vent to our imaginations and to the plan we mean to put into practice in our pastoral life."

o: Con esto, bajaron de la cuesta y se fueron a su pueblo.
t: With this, they came down the slope and made for their town.

o: De los agüeros que tuvo don Quijote al entrar de su aldea, con otros sucesos que adornan y acreditan esta grande historia.
t: Of the omens Don Quixote had upon entering his village, with other events that adorn and give credit to this great history.

o: A la entrada del cual, según dice Cide Hamete, vio don Quijote que en las eras del lugar estaban riñendo dos mochachos, y el uno dijo al otro.
t: At the entrance of it, according to Cide Hamete, Don Quixote saw that in the threshing floors of the place two boys were squaring, and one said to the other:

o: — No te canses Periquillo, que no la has de ver en todos los días de tu vida.
t: "Don't tire yourself out, Periquillo, for you won't see her in all the days of your life."

o: Oyólo don Quijote, y dijo a Sancho.
t: Don Quixote heard this, and said to Sancho:

o: — ¿No adviertes, amigo, lo que aquel mochacho ha dicho: ''no la has de ver en todos los días de tu vida''?
t: "Don't you notice, friend, what that boy has said: 'you won't see her in all the days of your life'?"

o: — Pues bien, ¿qué importa —respondió Sancho— que haya dicho eso el mochacho?
t: "Well, what does it matter," answered Sancho, "that the boy should have said that?"

o: — ¿Qué? —replicó don Quijote—.
t: "What?" replied Don Quixote.

o: ¿No vees tú que, aplicando aquella palabra a mi intención, quiere significar que no tengo de ver más a Dulcinea?
t: Don't you see that, applying that word to my meaning, he wants to signify that I am never to see Dulcinea again?

o: Queríale responder Sancho, cuando se lo estorbó ver que por aquella campaña venía huyendo una liebre, seguida de muchos galgos y cazadores, la cual, temerosa, se vino a recoger y a agazapar debajo de los pies del rucio.
t: Sancho was about to answer when he was interrupted by the sight of a hare coming across that field, followed by many hounds and hunters; the creature, frightened, took refuge and crouched down beneath the donkey's feet.

o: Cogióla Sancho a mano salva y presentósela a don Quijote, el cual estaba diciendo.
t: Sancho caught her up by hand and presented her to Don Quixote, who was saying:

o: Liebre huye, galgos la siguen: ¡Dulcinea no parece!
t: The hare flees, the hounds pursue her: Dulcinea is not to be seen!

o: — Estraño es vuesa merced —dijo Sancho—.
t: "Strange is it, your grace," said Sancho.

o: Presupongamos que esta liebre es Dulcinea del Toboso y estos galgos que la persiguen son los malandrines encantadores que la transformaron en labradora: ella huye, yo la cojo y la pongo en poder de vuesa merced, que la tiene en sus brazos y la regala: ¿qué mala señal es ésta, ni qué mal agüero se puede tomar de aquí?
t: Let us suppose this hare is Dulcinea of Toboso, and these hounds that pursue her are the rascally enchanters who transformed her into a peasant lass: she flees, I catch her, and I put her in your grace's power, who holds her in his arms and gives her away: what a bad sign is this, and what an ill omen can be drawn from it?"

o: Los dos mochachos de la pendencia se llegaron a ver la liebre, y al uno dellos preguntó Sancho que por qué reñían.
t: The two boys from the quarrel came up to the hare, and Sancho asked the one of them why they were fighting.

o: Y fuele respondido por el que había dicho ''no la verás más en toda tu vida'', que él había tomado al otro mochacho una jaula de grillos, la cual no pensaba volvérsela en toda su vida.
t: And he who had said "you will never see her again in all your life" was told in reply that the other boy had taken from him a cage of crickets, which he did not intend to give back to him as long as he lived.

o: Sacó Sancho cuatro cuartos de la faltriquera y dióselos al mochacho por la jaula, y púsosela en las manos a don Quijote, diciendo.
t: Sancho took four reales from his pouch and gave them to the boy for the cage, and then placed it in Don Quixote's hands, saying:

o: — He aquí, señor, rompidos y desbaratados estos agüeros, que no tienen que ver más con nuestros sucesos, según que yo imagino, aunque tonto, que con las nubes de antaño.
t: "Here, sir, are these omens broken and scattered, which, as I imagine, though a fool, have nothing more to do with our affairs than with the clouds of the other day."

o: Y si no me acuerdo mal, he oído decir al cura de nuestro pueblo que no es de personas cristianas ni discretas mirar en estas niñerías; y aun vuesa merced mismo me lo dijo los días pasados, dándome a entender que eran tontos todos aquellos cristianos que miraban en agüeros.
t: And if I remember rightly, I have heard our village priest say that it is neither the mark of Christian nor of discreet people to look into such trifles; and your grace yourself said the same to me the other day, giving me to understand that all those Christians who look into omens are fools.

o: Y no es menester hacer hincapié en esto, sino pasemos adelante y entremos en nuestra aldea.
t: And there is no need to dwell on this, but let us move on and enter our village.

o: Llegaron los cazadores, pidieron su liebre, y diósela don Quijote; pasaron adelante, y, a la entrada del pueblo, toparon en un pradecillo rezando al cura y al bachiller Carrasco.
t: The hunters arrived and asked for their hare, and Don Quixote gave it to them; they went on their way, and at the entrance of the village they came upon a little meadow where the priest and the bachelor Carrasco were saying their prayers.

o: Y es de saber que Sancho Panza había echado sobre el rucio y sobre el lío de las armas, para que sirviese de repostero, la túnica de bocací, pintada de llamas de fuego que le vistieron en el castillo del duque la noche que volvió en sí Altisidora.
t: It should be known that Sancho Panza had laid over the donkey and over the bundle of armor, to serve as a pageant-drapery, the coarse cloth tunic painted with flames of fire which they had dressed him in at the duke's castle the night that Altisidora came to her senses.

o: Acomodóle también la coroza en la cabeza, que fue la más nueva transformación y adorno con que se vio jamás jumento en el mundo.
t: He also fitted the crown on his head, which was the newest transformation and adornment ever seen on a donkey in the world.

o: Fueron luego conocidos los dos del cura y del bachiller, que se vinieron a ellos con los brazos abiertos.
t: The priest and the bachelor were soon recognized, and they came toward them with open arms.

o: Apeóse don Quijote y abrazólos estrechamente; y los mochachos, que son linces no escusados, divisaron la coroza del jumento y acudieron a verle, y decían unos a otros.
t: Don Quixote dismounted and embraced them closely; and the boys, who are unashamed linnets, spied the crown on the donkey and came to look at it, saying to one another:

o: — Venid, mochachos, y veréis el asno de Sancho Panza más galán que Mingo, y la bestia de don Quijote más flaca hoy que el primer día.
t: "Come, boys, and you will see Sancho Panza's ass more gallant than Mingo, and Don Quixote's beast leaner today than on the first day."

o: Finalmente, rodeados de mochachos y acompañados del cura y del bachiller, entraron en el pueblo, y se fueron a casa de don Quijote, y hallaron a la puerta della al ama y a su sobrina, a quien ya habían llegado las nuevas de su venida.
t: Finally, surrounded by boys and accompanied by the priest and the bachelor, they entered the village and went to Don Quixote's house, and at its door they found the housekeeper and his niece, who had already been told of his coming.

o: Ni más ni menos se las habían dado a Teresa Panza, mujer de Sancho, la cual, desgreñada y medio desnuda, trayendo de la mano a Sanchica, su hija, acudió a ver a su marido; y, viéndole no tan bien adeliñado como ella se pensaba que había de estar un gobernador, le dijo.
t: They had given the news to Teresa Panza, Sancho's wife, no sooner nor later; and she, disheveled and half naked, leading her daughter Sanchica by the hand, came to see her husband; and seeing him not so well turned out as she had supposed a governor ought to be, she said:

o: — ¿Cómo venís así, marido mío, que me parece que venís a pie y despeado, y más traéis semejanza de desgobernado que de gobernador?
t: "How come you like this, my husband? It seems to me you are on foot and footsore, and you bear more the likeness of one deposed than of a governor."

o: — Calla, Teresa —respondió Sancho—, que muchas veces donde hay estacas no hay tocinos, y vámonos a nuestra casa, que allá oirás maravillas.
t: "Quiet down, Teresa," Sancho replied, "for many a time there's more stumps than bacon, and let's go home, for there you'll hear wonders."

o: Dineros traigo, que es lo que importa, ganados por mi industria y sin daño de nadie.
t: "I've brought money, which is what matters, earned by my own labor and harm to no one."

o: — Traed vos dinero, mi buen marido —dijo Teresa—, y sean ganados por aquí o por allí, que, comoquiera que los hayáis ganado, no habréis hecho usanza nueva en el mundo.
t: "Bring money, my good husband," said Teresa, "whether earned here or there; however you may have earned it, you won't have set a new fashion in the world."

o: Abrazó Sanchica a su padre, y preguntóle si traía algo, que le estaba esperando como el agua de mayo; y, asiéndole de un lado del cinto, y su mujer de la mano, tirando su hija al rucio, se fueron a su casa, dejando a don Quijote en la suya, en poder de su sobrina y de su ama, y en compañía del cura y del bachiller.
t: Sanchica embraced her father and asked if he had brought anything, for she had been waiting for him like the May rain; and, taking him by one side of his belt and his wife by the hand, and setting his daughter up on the donkey, they went off to their house, leaving Don Quixote in his own, in the care of his niece and his housekeeper, and in the company of the curate and the bachelor.

o: Díjole el cura que los dijese.
t: The curate told him to say it.

o: Respondió don Quijote que él se había de llamar el pastor Quijotiz; y el bachiller, el pastor Carrascón; y el cura, el pastor Curambro; y Sancho Panza, el pastor Pancino.
t: Don Quixote answered that he would call himself the shepherd Quijotiz; and the bachelor, the shepherd Carrascón; and the curate, the shepherd Curambro; and Sancho Panza, the shepherd Pancino.

o: Pasmáronse todos de ver la nueva locura de don Quijote; pero, porque no se les fuese otra vez del pueblo a sus caballerías, esperando que en aquel año podría ser curado, concedieron con su nueva intención, y aprobaron por discreta su locura, ofreciéndosele por compañeros en su ejercicio.
t: They were all astounded at the new madness of Don Quixote; but, so that he might not go off to his escapades again out of the village, hoping that in that year he might be cured, they granted him his new notion and approved his folly as sensible, offering themselves as his companions in his exercise.

o: — Eso está de molde —respondió don Quijote—, puesto que yo estoy libre de buscar nombre de pastora fingida, pues está ahí la sin par Dulcinea del Toboso, gloria de estas riberas, adorno de estos prados, sustento de la hermosura, nata de los donaires, y, finalmente, sujeto sobre quien puede asentar bien toda alabanza, por hipérbole que sea.
t: "That fits the pattern," Don Quixote replied, "since I am free to seek no name for a feigned shepherdess, for there is there the peerless Dulcinea of Toboso, glory of these banks, adornment of these meadows, sustenance of beauty, cream of wit, and, in short, a subject on which every praise may rest well, be it by way of hyperbole."

o: — Así es verdad —dijo el cura—, pero nosotros buscaremos por ahí pastoras mañeruelas, que si no nos cuadraren, nos esquinen.
t: "That's true enough," said the curate, "but we'll look for some rustic shepherdesses thereabouts, and if they don't suit us, they'll give us the cold shoulder."

o: A lo que añadió Sansón Carrasco.
t: To which Samson Carrasco added.

o: — Y cuando faltaren, darémosles los nombres de las estampadas e impresas, de quien está lleno el mundo: Fílidas, Amarilis, Dianas, Fléridas, Galateas y Belisardas; que, pues las venden en las plazas, bien las podemos comprar nosotros y tenerlas por nuestras.
t: "And when they run out, we'll give them the names of the ones stamped and printed, of those the world is full of: Phyllis, Amarillis, Diana, Floridas, Galatea and Belisarda; for since they're sold in the squares, we can buy them ourselves and have them as our own."

o: Si mi dama, o, por mejor decir, mi pastora, por ventura se llamare Ana, la celebraré debajo del nombre de Anarda; y si Francisca, la llamaré yo Francenia; y si Lucía, Lucinda, que todo se sale allá; y Sancho Panza, si es que ha de entrar en esta cofadría, podrá celebrar a su mujer Teresa Panza con nombre de Teresaina.
t: If my lady, or, better said, my shepherdess, should happen to be called Anne, I'll celebrate her under the name of Anarda; and if Frances, I'll call her Francenia; and if Lucy, Lucinda, for everything is turned that way; and Sancho Panza, if he is to join this brotherhood, may celebrate his wife Teresa Panza under the name of Teresaina.

o: Rióse don Quijote de la aplicación del nombre, y el cura le alabó infinito su honesta y honrada resolución, y se ofreció de nuevo a hacerle compañía todo el tiempo que le vacase de atender a sus forzosas obligaciones.
t: Don Quixote laughed at the application of the name, and the curate praised his honest and honorable resolve without end, and offered anew to keep him company for as long as he was free from his unavoidable duties.

o: Con esto, se despidieron dél, y le rogaron y aconsejaron tuviese cuenta con su salud, con regalarse lo que fuese bueno.
t: With this they took their leave of him, and begged and advised him to look after his health, and to indulge himself in whatever was good.

o: Quiso la suerte que su sobrina y el ama oyeron la plática de los tres; y, así como se fueron, se entraron entrambas con don Quijote, y la sobrina le dijo.
t: Luck would have it that his niece and the housekeeper overheard the talk of the three; and as soon as they had gone, the two of them came in to Don Quixote, and the niece said to him.

o: — ¿Qué es esto, señor tío?
t: "What is this, uncle?"

o: ¿Ahora que pensábamos nosotras que vuestra merced volvía a reducirse en su casa, y pasar en ella una vida quieta y honrada, se quiere meter en nuevos laberintos, haciéndose.
t: "Now that we thought, sir, that your grace was going to settle down again in your house and lead a quiet and honest life there, you mean to plunge into new labyrinths, making yourself..."

o: Pastorcillo, tú que vienes, pastorcico, tú que vas?
t: Little shepherd, you who come, little shepherd, you who go?

o: Pues en verdad que está ya duro el alcacel para zampoñas.
t: "For truly, the bagpipe is already hard enough for rustic pipes."

o: A lo que añadió el ama.
t: To which the housekeeper added.

o: Y ¿podrá vuestra merced pasar en el campo las siestas del verano, los serenos del invierno, el aullido de los lobos?
t: And could your grace spend the summer afternoons in the fields, the winter nights without fire, the howling of the wolves?

o: No, por cierto, que éste es ejercicio y oficio de hombres robustos, curtidos y criados para tal ministerio casi desde las fajas y mantillas.
t: No, certainly not, for that is the exercise and calling of robust men, toughened and raised for such a ministry almost from the cradle.

o: Aun, mal por mal, mejor es ser caballero andante que pastor.
t: Still, bad as it is, better to be a knight-errant than a shepherd.

o: Mire, señor, tome mi consejo, que no se le doy sobre estar harta de pan y vino, sino en ayunas, y sobre cincuenta años que tengo de edad: estése en su casa, atienda a su hacienda, confiese a menudo, favorezca a los pobres, y sobre mi ánima si mal le fuere.
t: Look, sir, take my advice; I give it not because you are sick of bread and wine, but because I am fasting, and because I am fifty years old: stay in your house, look after your estate, confess often, favor the poor, and, for my soul's sake, if anything should befall you.

o: — Callad, hijas —les respondió don Quijote—, que yo sé bien lo que me cumple.
t: "Be quiet, daughters," Don Quixote replied, "for I know well what is required of me."

o: Llevadme al lecho, que me parece que no estoy muy bueno, y tened por cierto que, ahora sea caballero andante o pastor por andar, no dejaré siempre de acudir a lo que hubiéredes menester, como lo veréis por la obra.
t: Take me to bed, for I feel I am not very well; and rest assured that, whether knight-errant or shepherd for the sake of walking, I shall never fail to come to whatever you may need, as you will see in the deed.

o: Y las buenas hijas —que lo eran sin duda ama y sobrina— le llevaron a la cama, donde le dieron de comer y regalaron lo posible.
t: And the good daughters—which without doubt were his housekeeper and niece—took him to bed, where they gave him to eat and treated him as well as they could.
